core: Working definition of INSERT, attributed: W3Schools says the INSERT INTO statement is used to insert new records in a table; PostgreSQL says the INSERT statement is used to populate a table with rows; SQLite says the VALUES form creates one or more new rows in an existing table

Basic anatomy: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values) — the table name plus a column list and a VALUES list, per W3Schools syntax; original example INSERT INTO products (name, price, quantity) VALUES ('Ridge tent', 129.99, 24);

Column order and matching: values line up with the listed columns in the same order; per SQLite the number of values must match the number of specified columns; listing columns explicitly lets you reorder or omit columns (PostgreSQL), and omitted columns get their default value or NULL (SQLite)

What happens to the primary key: the database assigns a new value (auto-increment fields are automatically generated when a new record is inserted, W3Schools) or checks a supplied value against the key's uniqueness requirement; primary-keys is a sibling topic, referenced only

INSERT and constraints: SQL lets you define constraints on columns and tables, and if a user attempts to store data that would violate a constraint, an error is raised (PostgreSQL) — the row never lands; data-integrity is a sibling topic, referenced only

Writing versus reading: a SELECT statement does not make any changes to the database (SQLite), while INSERT creates new rows in an existing table (SQLite) — INSERT changes stored data permanently; select is a sibling topic, referenced only
Honest framing: INSERT is how data enters the database, and mistakes are hard to undo — removing or repairing a bad row takes another write command (delete/update, sibling topics)
supporting: The bare VALUES form without a column list requires the values to match the table's column order (W3Schools, PostgreSQL)
Many developers consider explicitly listing the columns better style than relying on the implicit order (PostgreSQL)
A primary key constraint ensures unique values and cannot contain NULL values (W3Schools)
Statements end with a semicolon in standard usage (PostgreSQL tutorial)
outOfScope: Data types and their input formats (own topic: data-types)
Primary key design in depth (own topic: primary-keys)
Constraint catalog and data-quality enforcement in depth (own topic: data-integrity)

claims.claim: W3Schools defines the INSERT INTO statement as the statement used to insert new records in a table.
PostgreSQL's tutorial states that the INSERT statement is used to populate a table with rows; the first examples use the bare form INSERT INTO table VALUES (...).
SQLite's documentation describes the VALUES form of INSERT as creating one or more new rows in an existing table.

The basic shape of an INSERT is INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values): W3Schools documents the two-list syntax (column names and the values to be inserted), and PostgreSQL presents listing the columns explicitly as the alternative to the bare VALUES form.

Values must line up with the listed columns: SQLite states that when a column-name list is specified, the number of values must match the number of specified columns, and PostgreSQL notes the bare syntax requires remembering the order of the columns while an explicit list lets you reorder or omit columns.
Columns omitted from an INSERT's column list are populated with the column's default value, or with NULL if no default is specified (SQLite).

A database may assign the primary key itself: W3Schools explains that an auto-increment field is automatically generated when a new record is inserted; if a key value is supplied, it is checked, because a primary key constraint ensures unique values.
INSERT is where constraints are enforced: PostgreSQL states that if a user attempts to store data in a column that would violate a constraint, an error is raised — the row is rejected.

INSERT is a write operation: SQLite's SELECT reference states that a SELECT statement does not make any changes to the database, while its INSERT reference describes INSERT as creating new rows — the stored table changes permanently.

Honest framing: INSERT is how data enters the database, and because it writes, a mistaken row is hard to undo — an interpretive framing built on the write-versus-read distinction documented by SQLite and the add-rows definitions of W3Schools and PostgreSQL.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources phrase the same operation differently: W3Schools says INSERT inserts new records in a table, PostgreSQL says INSERT populates a table with rows, and SQLite says the VALUES form creates one or more new rows in an existing table.
positions: W3Schools: 'insert new records in a table'
SQLite: 'creates one or more new rows in an existing table'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three describe the same operation: adding rows to a table. The lesson uses the add-a-row wording as its working definition, attributed to W3Schools and PostgreSQL, with SQLite's phrasing as the same idea stated for its own documentation.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. An alternative syntax allows you to list the columns explicitly'; 'You can list the columns in a different order if you wish or even omit some columns'; 'Many developers consider explicitly listing the columns better style than relying on the order implicitly'. sourceRecords.title: SQLite Query Language: INSERT
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: 'The first form (with the "VALUES" keyword) creates one or more new rows in an existing table'; 'If a column-name list is specified, then the number of values in each term of the VALUE list must match the number of specified columns'; omitted columns 'are populated with the default column value ... or with NULL if no default value is specified'. Used for the add-a-row definition, the matching rule, and the omitted-columns behavior.
